courseDesc: Learn what malicious bots are, how they work, the dangers they create, and how to protect yourself and your devices from automated cyberattacks.

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is a bot?
choices: An automated program that performs tasks
A physical robot that repairs computers
A type of computer virus
A human who works online

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What makes a bot malicious?
choices: It operates automatically
It is designed to perform harmful or unwanted actions
It connects to the internet
It is used by a company

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Are all bots malicious?
choices: Yes, every bot is dangerous
No, many bots perform useful and legitimate tasks
Yes, but only on social media
No, because bots cannot cause harm

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is one example of a legitimate bot?
choices: A bot that steals passwords
A bot that floods a website with requests
A search engine crawler that indexes websites
A bot that sends fraudulent messages

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Why are bots useful to attackers?
choices: They can automate tasks and perform them at large scale
They make computers impossible to hack
They automatically repair damaged websites
They prevent people from accessing the internet

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is automation?
choices: Manually completing every computer task
Using technology to perform tasks automatically
Turning off a computer permanently
Deleting all online accounts

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: How can malicious bots affect ordinary internet users?
choices: They can never affect ordinary users
They can steal account information, spread scams, or disrupt services
They only affect large technology companies
They only damage computer hardware

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is a botnet?
choices: A network of connected websites
A group of compromised devices controlled together
A type of secure password
A legitimate search engine

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is a device that has been infected and added to a botnet sometimes called?
choices: A zombie device
A firewall
A password manager
A search crawler

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Why might someone not realize their device is part of a botnet?
choices: The device may continue to work normally while being misused in the background
Botnets only use devices that are turned off
Botnets always display a warning message
A botnet makes every device visibly change color

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is the main difference between a human-operated attack and a bot attack?
choices: Bot attacks can automate repetitive actions at very large scale
Human attacks always cause more damage
Bot attacks cannot connect to the internet
There is no difference in how they operate

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Can malicious bots operate without someone manually controlling every action?
choices: No, every action requires a person
Yes, they can automatically follow programmed instructions
Only when the internet is disconnected
Only on mobile phones

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Why might cybercriminals use many bots instead of just one?
choices: To make attacks larger and harder to stop
To reduce the speed of their attacks
To make their activity completely harmless
To avoid using computers

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: What is one way malicious bots can be distributed?
choices: Through compromised devices and malware infections
Only through official app stores
Only through computer keyboards
Through printed books

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Can a malicious bot target a website without directly infecting the visitor's computer?
choices: Yes, it can send automated requests to the website
No, every bot must infect every visitor
Only if the website is offline
Only if the visitor downloads a file

What Are Malicious Bots?.question: Explain what a malicious bot is and how it differs from a legitimate bot.
What is a botnet, and why can it be dangerous?

courseModules.moduleTitle: 2. Three Common Types of Malicious Bots

DDoS Bots.question: What does DDoS stand for?
choices: Distributed Denial of Service
Digital Data Operating System
Direct Device Online Security
Distributed Data Operating Software

DDoS Bots.question: What is the main goal of a DDoS attack?
choices: To make a website or online service unavailable
To improve a website's speed
To create stronger passwords
To organize files on a computer

DDoS Bots.question: How do DDoS bots commonly help carry out an attack?
choices: By sending large numbers of requests from many devices
By repairing the target website
By deleting the internet
By making every visitor log out

DDoS Bots.question: Why is a DDoS attack called distributed?
choices: Because traffic comes from multiple devices or sources
Because it only affects one computer
Because it is spread across different passwords
Because it is performed by one person manually

DDoS Bots.question: What might happen to a website during a successful DDoS attack?
choices: It may become extremely slow or unavailable
It automatically becomes more secure
It gains unlimited storage
It stops needing a server

DDoS Bots.question: Why can DDoS attacks be difficult to stop?
choices: They can involve large amounts of traffic from many sources
They only use one easily identifiable computer
They do not use internet connections
They always happen when a website is offline

DDoS Bots.question: Who can be affected by a DDoS attack?
choices: Websites, businesses, organizations, and their users
Only people who own servers
Only social media influencers
Nobody outside the attacker's computer

DDoS Bots.question: What is one possible consequence of a DDoS attack on an online store?
choices: Customers may be unable to shop or complete purchases
Products automatically become cheaper
The store receives unlimited new customers
The store no longer needs internet access

Spam Bots.question: What is a spam bot?
choices: A bot that automatically sends or posts unwanted messages
A bot that protects passwords
A bot that repairs websites
A bot that improves internet connections

Spam Bots.question: Where might spam bots operate?
choices: Email, social media, websites, and messaging platforms
Only inside computer processors
Only on offline computers
Only in government buildings

Spam Bots.question: What might a spam bot send?
choices: Unwanted advertisements, scams, or malicious links
Only personal messages from friends
Only official security updates
Only computer repair instructions

Spam Bots.question: Why do attackers use spam bots?
choices: To spread messages to large numbers of people automatically
To make email inboxes safer
To stop people from receiving messages
To improve website privacy

Spam Bots.question: What is one danger of clicking a link sent by a spam bot?
choices: It could lead to a phishing page or malware download
It always makes your device faster
It automatically verifies your identity
It permanently protects your account

Spam Bots.question: What might a spam bot do on a social media platform?
choices: Post repeated advertisements or fake comments
Automatically verify every user
Prevent all fake accounts
Remove every suspicious website

Spam Bots.question: Why can spam bots make it difficult to use an online platform?
choices: They can fill discussions and inboxes with unwanted content
They make all messages disappear
They prevent users from creating passwords
They turn every account into an administrator

Spam Bots.question: What is one sign that a social media account might be automated spam?
choices: It repeatedly posts identical or suspicious messages
It has a profile picture
It follows a friend
It posts an occasional photograph

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: What is credential stuffing?
choices: Using stolen username-and-password combinations to try to access accounts
Creating a new password for every website
Storing passwords in a password manager
Encrypting files to protect them

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: Where do attackers often get the stolen credentials used in credential stuffing?
choices: Data breaches and stolen account databases
Official password safety guides
Public weather reports
Computer instruction manuals

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: Why does credential stuffing sometimes work?
choices: People reuse the same passwords across different websites
All websites share one password
Passwords never expire
Websites automatically reveal passwords

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: How do credential stuffing bots help attackers?
choices: They automatically test stolen login combinations at scale
They create secure passwords for victims
They block unauthorized logins
They repair compromised accounts

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: What might happen if a credential stuffing attack succeeds?
choices: An attacker may gain access to someone's account
The victim automatically gets a new password
The account becomes impossible to access
The website deletes all user information

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: Which account could be at risk from credential stuffing?
choices: An email, banking, shopping, or social media account
Only an account with no password
Only an offline notebook
Only an account owned by a website developer

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: Why is using the same password on many websites dangerous?
choices: One stolen password may unlock multiple accounts
It makes every account more secure
It prevents data breaches
It makes passwords impossible to guess

Credential Stuffing Bots.question: What security feature can make stolen passwords less useful to attackers?
choices: Multi-factor authentication
Using the same password everywhere
Sharing passwords with friends
Turning off account notifications

Comparing the Three Types.question: Which type of bot is mainly associated with overwhelming a website with traffic?
choices: DDoS bot
Spam bot
Credential stuffing bot
Search engine crawler

Comparing the Three Types.question: Which type of bot is mainly associated with sending unwanted messages?
choices: Spam bot
DDoS bot
Credential stuffing bot
Backup bot

Comparing the Three Types.question: Which type of bot is mainly associated with trying stolen login information?
choices: Credential stuffing bot
Spam bot
DDoS bot
Search engine crawler

Comparing the Three Types.question: A website receives huge amounts of automated traffic and becomes unavailable. Which attack is most likely happening?
choices: DDoS attack
Credential stuffing attack
Spam campaign
Password reset

Comparing the Three Types.question: An online platform is flooded with fake comments advertising suspicious websites. What is most likely responsible?
choices: Spam bots
DDoS bots
Credential stuffing bots
Legitimate search crawlers

Comparing the Three Types.question: A user's account receives many login attempts using combinations of previously leaked passwords. What is this likely to be?
choices: Credential stuffing
A DDoS attack
A spam campaign
A software update

Comparing the Three Types.question: Can the three types of malicious bots be used together in a larger cyberattack?
choices: Yes, attackers can combine different automated activities
No, they cannot operate at the same time
Only spam bots can work with other bots
No, because all bots have identical purposes

Comparing the Three Types.question: Explain the difference between DDoS bots, spam bots, and credential stuffing bots.

courseModules.moduleTitle: 3. Why You Should Be Concerned About Malicious Bots

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why should ordinary people be concerned about malicious bots?
choices: They can threaten accounts, personal information, and access to online services
They only affect large technology companies
They cannot affect people who use the internet
They only operate on government networks

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: What could happen if a bot successfully accesses someone's email account?
choices: The attacker could access private messages and potentially reset other account passwords
The account becomes permanently safer
The attacker automatically loses internet access
Nothing, because email accounts contain no useful information

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: How can malicious bots contribute to financial loss?
choices: By helping attackers steal accounts, commit fraud, or disrupt businesses
By automatically refunding every purchase
By preventing all online transactions
By making every website free

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why might a business be seriously affected by a DDoS attack?
choices: Customers may be unable to access its services, causing lost revenue
The business automatically gains more customers
Its products become unavailable everywhere permanently
The attack improves its website performance

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: How can spam bots put people at risk?
choices: They can distribute phishing links and fraudulent messages
They automatically remove suspicious emails
They prevent all online scams
They make passwords stronger

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: What is one possible result of credential stuffing against a banking account?
choices: Unauthorized access that could lead to financial harm
Automatic protection against fraud
A guaranteed increase in account security
The bank automatically closes every account

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: How can malicious bots affect a company's reputation?
choices: Customers may lose trust if services are disrupted or accounts are compromised
They always improve customer satisfaction
They automatically increase positive reviews
They prevent customers from discussing the company

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why can bot attacks be expensive for organizations?
choices: They may require security investigations, recovery work, and service improvements
They automatically pay the organization's bills
They eliminate the need for technology
They only affect free services

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Can malicious bots be used to manipulate online information?
choices: Yes, they can generate fake comments, engagement, and misleading activity
No, bots cannot post online
Only human users can create fake engagement
No, because every online account is verified

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: What is fake engagement?
choices: Artificial likes, comments, views, or followers created to mislead people
A real conversation between friends
A secure login process
A software update

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why might attackers want to steal online accounts?
choices: To steal information, impersonate users, commit fraud, or access other accounts
To help users remember passwords
To make every account private
To improve website design

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Can malicious bots affect services that people depend on every day?
choices: Yes, attacks can disrupt websites, communication, shopping, and other online services
No, they only affect unused websites
Only if a person downloads a bot
No, because online services cannot be attacked

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why can a botnet be more dangerous than a single compromised device?
choices: Many devices can act together and create a much larger impact
A botnet can only affect one website
It automatically removes malware
It prevents attackers from communicating

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: What is one reason malicious bot activity can be difficult to investigate?
choices: Activity may come from many devices and locations
Bots always reveal the attacker's identity
Bots never leave any network activity
Every bot uses the same device

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Why should people take suspicious automated activity seriously even if they have not lost money?
choices: It may be an early sign of attempted account compromise or fraud
It proves that every account is already stolen
It means the internet is permanently broken
It guarantees that no harm can happen

The Consequences of Malicious Bots.question: Describe two ways malicious bots can harm individuals and two ways they can harm businesses.

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Which of the following could be a warning sign of a credential stuffing attack?
choices: Repeated failed login attempts from unfamiliar locations or devices
A normal successful login from your usual device
Receiving a regular software update
Changing your profile picture

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: What might indicate that a website is experiencing a DDoS attack?
choices: Unusually slow performance or widespread service unavailability
A normal website loading quickly
A scheduled maintenance announcement
A new article appearing on the homepage

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: What could indicate spam bot activity in an online discussion?
choices: Many repetitive comments containing suspicious links
A few genuine comments from different users
A moderator answering a question
A user posting an original photograph

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Why should you be suspicious of messages sent by accounts with repetitive behavior?
choices: They may be automated accounts distributing spam or scams
Every repetitive message is guaranteed to be safe
It proves the account belongs to a company
It means the message has been verified

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: What should you do if you receive an unexpected login notification?
choices: Check the account through its official app or website and secure it if necessary
Ignore it no matter what
Click any link in the notification immediately
Share your password with the sender

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: What could repeated password reset emails that you did not request indicate?
choices: Someone may be attempting to access or interfere with your account
Your password is guaranteed to be stolen
Your device has automatically been repaired
The emails are always harmless advertisements

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Why is it important to distinguish between a legitimate bot and a malicious bot?
choices: Not all automated activity is harmful, so context matters
Every bot should be treated as a criminal
Legitimate bots cannot be identified
Only malicious bots use automation

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: A website suddenly receives thousands of requests and stops responding. What should its administrators investigate?
choices: A possible DDoS attack or other unusual traffic surge
A normal password change
A user's profile picture
A harmless email attachment

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: An account posts the same promotional link hundreds of times. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Automated spam activity
A normal software update
A password manager
A legitimate security alert

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: You receive an alert about a login attempt from an unfamiliar device. What is the safest first step?
choices: Access the service directly through its official website or app to investigate
Reply to the alert with your password
Click a suspicious link to cancel the login
Post the alert publicly with your account details

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Why might a sudden increase in failed login attempts be important?
choices: It could indicate automated attempts to guess or reuse credentials
It proves that your account has no password
It means your device is fully protected
It always happens after a software update

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Can one unusual event prove that a malicious bot is responsible?
choices: No, unusual activity should be investigated in context
Yes, every unusual event is caused by a bot
Yes, if the website is slow
No, because bots never create unusual activity

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Why should organizations monitor traffic and login patterns?
choices: To identify unusual behavior and investigate possible attacks
To make all accounts public
To prevent users from accessing their services
To automatically delete all customer information

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: What information might help a security team investigate suspicious bot activity?
choices: Relevant timestamps, traffic patterns, login records, and security logs
Only the website's logo
The personal opinions of random users
The color of a computer screen

Warning Signs and Suspicious Activity.question: Explain three warning signs that could indicate malicious bot activity.
Why is unusual online activity not always proof of a cyberattack?

courseModules.moduleTitle: 5. Preventing and Responding to Malicious Bots

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is one of the best ways to protect yourself from credential stuffing?
choices: Use a unique password for every account
Use the same password everywhere
Share passwords with friends
Choose very short passwords

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Why should you enable multi-factor authentication?
choices: It adds another layer of protection beyond your password
It makes every password public
It prevents all internet traffic
It removes the need for account security

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is a password manager useful for?
choices: Creating and storing strong, unique passwords
Sending passwords to strangers
Automatically posting online advertisements
Disabling account security

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should you do if you receive suspicious messages from a spam bot?
choices: Avoid clicking links and report or block the account
Click every link to see where it goes
Share the message with all your contacts
Send the account your login information

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should you do if you suspect someone has accessed your account?
choices: Change your password using the official service and review account security
Ignore the activity
Send your password to the person who contacted you
Delete all your security notifications

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Why is it important to keep software and devices updated?
choices: Updates can fix security vulnerabilities that attackers may exploit
Updates guarantee that no attack can ever happen
Updates make passwords unnecessary
Updates prevent every website from using bots

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should you do if your device may have been infected and added to a botnet?
choices: Disconnect it from the network if appropriate and use trusted security tools or professional help
Ignore all warnings
Install random software advertised in a message
Share the device with more people

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Why should you avoid downloading software from untrusted websites?
choices: It may contain malware that could compromise your device
It always improves device security
It automatically removes malicious bots
It guarantees faster internet access

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is one way a website can defend itself against DDoS attacks?
choices: Use DDoS protection and traffic filtering services
Share its administrator password publicly
Disable every security feature
Allow unlimited requests from every source

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is rate limiting?
choices: Restricting how many requests a user or system can make in a period of time
Allowing unlimited requests from every device
Changing a website's background color
Removing all user accounts

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: How can a website reduce automated spam?
choices: Use moderation, spam filtering, and appropriate bot-detection measures
Allow every message without review
Publish users' passwords
Disable all account protections

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is a CAPTCHA commonly used for?
choices: Helping distinguish human users from automated activity
Storing passwords in plain text
Making websites impossible to access
Automatically repairing infected devices

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Does CAPTCHA stop every malicious bot?
choices: No, it is one defensive measure and can sometimes be bypassed
Yes, it stops every automated attack
Yes, it eliminates the need for all security
No, because it only works offline

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should an organization do when it detects suspicious automated login attempts?
choices: Investigate the activity and apply appropriate protections such as rate limits and stronger authentication
Publish its user passwords
Ignore every login alert
Disable all account security

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Why is it useful to report malicious bot accounts to a platform?
choices: The platform may investigate and remove accounts violating its rules
It automatically deletes the entire internet
It guarantees that the attacker will be identified
It makes the account more trustworthy

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should you do if you receive a security alert about a suspicious login?
choices: Verify it through the official service and secure your account if needed
Send your password to the alert sender
Click an unfamiliar link without checking it
Ignore it permanently

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Why should you review active sessions on important accounts?
choices: You may find unfamiliar devices or sessions that should be signed out
It automatically removes all malware from your computer
It makes passwords unnecessary
It prevents every DDoS attack

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What is the safest approach if a website you use is unavailable during a possible DDoS attack?
choices: Wait for official updates and avoid suspicious links claiming to restore access
Download an unknown repair program
Share your login information with strangers
Repeatedly enter your password on unofficial websites

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: A friend tells you to use the same password on every website because it is easier to remember. What should you explain?
choices: Password reuse makes credential stuffing more dangerous
Password reuse prevents data breaches
All websites automatically share passwords
Unique passwords are less secure

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Which statement best describes protection against malicious bots?
choices: Multiple security measures work together to reduce risk
One security tool can stop every bot forever
Only large companies need protection
There is nothing anyone can do

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: What should you do if your account has been compromised and you reused its password elsewhere?
choices: Change that password on every other account where it was reused
Keep using the same password
Share the password with friends
Turn off multi-factor authentication

Protecting Yourself and Your Accounts.question: Explain three ways individuals can protect themselves from malicious bots.
